identity.title: 14-3-3 Enables beta-Adrenergic Regulation of the Cardiac Sodium Channel at the Intercalated Disc.

content.abstract: BACKGROUND: beta-Adrenergic stimulation enables the heart to adapt electrical activity to increased physiological demand. Although the cardiac sodium channel Na(v)1.5 is essential for impulse propagation, the mechanisms underlying its acute beta-adrenergic regulation, particularly within distinct cardiomyocyte membrane domains, remain poorly understood. We investigated whether the phosphorylation-sensitive adaptor protein 14-3-3 mediates this regulation. METHODS AND RESULTS: Using automated patch-clamp electrophysiology in HEK293 cells and human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs), we found that isoproterenol rapidly increased sodium current (I(Na)) and promoted channel activation at more hyperpolarized potentials, whereas PKA inhibition reduced I(Na). Disruption of 14-3-3 function abolished these responses without substantially altering basal sodium current or Na(v)1.5 surface expression. Macropatch recordings from ventricular myocytes revealed that isoproterenol preferentially enhanced I(Na) at the intercalated disc, an effect prevented by 14-3-3 inhibition. Proximity ligation assays further demonstrated increased Na(v)1.5/14-3-3 proximity following beta-adrenergic stimulation. Systematic mutagenesis identified S460 in the Na(v)1.5 DI-DII linker as a critical determinant of acute PKA-dependent regulation. Molecular modeling predicted that S460 phosphorylation stabilizes the Na(v)1.5/14-3-3 interaction. In CRISPR-engineered S460A iPSC-CMs, acute beta-adrenergic regulation of I(Na) was abolished, whereas the isoproterenol-induced increase in conduction velocity was significantly attenuated. Computational simulations further predicted that enhanced intercalated-disc sodium current supports increased conduction velocity across varying conditions of electrical coupling and pacing rate. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings identify 14-3-3 and S460 as critical determinants of spatially selective beta-adrenergic regulation of Na(v)1.5 at the cardiac intercalated disc. This mechanism provides a molecular link between sympathetic signaling and cardiac sodium current regulation, supporting the concept that localized enhancement of Na(v)1.5 function contributes to the adaptation of cardiac conduction during increased sympathetic demand.
